examNotes: Exam Tip 1: Theory answers should state BOTH $J = F\Delta t$ and $J = \Delta p$ and connect them — one-line answers lose marks.
Exam Tip 2: In numericals, convert grams to kg and quote directions ('opposite to initial motion') with magnitudes.
Exam Tip 3: Graph-reading impulse questions: label the base and height you used to compute the area.
Exam Tip 4: Safety-device explanations score full marks only with the chain: fixed $\Delta p$ → longer $\Delta t$ → smaller $F_{avg}$.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: Rebounds: add the speeds in $\Delta p = m(v_f + v_i)$ — sign flip doubles the effect.
Trick 2: 'Soft landing' MCQs: longer $\Delta t$ ⇒ smaller $F$ ⇒ pick the option that stretches the time.
Trick 3: Recoil from rest: $V = mv/M$ instantly, with $V$ opposite the bullet.
Trick 4: Machine-gun/stream problems: average force = mass flow rate × exit speed ($n\,mv$).
Trick 5: If a force–time curve has no nice shape, the answer is still its AREA — estimate with boxes if needed.
Trick 6: Impulsive force problems: always look for the 'short time' keyword — it implies $F_{avg} = \Delta p/\Delta t$ is the intended approach.
practiceQuestions: Q1. Define linear momentum and impulse, and state the relation between them.
Q2. Show that Newton's second law can be written as $F = dp/dt$ and state when this reduces to $F = ma$.
Q3. A 0.3 kg ball moving at 15 m/s is hit back along the same path at 25 m/s. Find the impulse delivered.
Q4. Explain, using the impulse–momentum theorem, why a crumple zone reduces injury in a crash.
Q5. From a given force–time graph (triangle), determine the final velocity of the struck body.
Q6. A 2 kg object is subjected to a force $F = 10t$ N. Find the change in momentum in 3 seconds.
Q7. Compare the impulse delivered by a constant force of 10 N for 5 s and a force $F = 2t$ for 5 s.
practice: A 60 kg runner at 8 m/s is stopped in 0.5 s. Find the impulse and the average force. — $J = 480$ kg·m/s; $F = 960$ N.
A 0.5 kg ball hits a wall at 12 m/s and rebounds at 8 m/s. Find the impulse. — $\Delta p = 0.5(8+12) = 10$ kg·m/s BACKWARD (note the sign reversal!).
From a triangular $F$–$t$ pulse peaking at 400 N over 0.02 s, find the impulse delivered to a 0.2 kg ball at rest. — Area $= \frac{1}{2}(0.02)(400) = 4$ N·s → $v = 20$ m/s.
A 1000 kg car at 20 m/s crashes into a barrier that stops it in 0.4 s. Find the average force, and compare with a crumple-zone stop in 1.0 s. — 50 kN vs 20 kN.
A machine-gun fires 30 g bullets at 400 m/s, 10 per second. Find the average recoil force. — $F = n\,mv = 10 \times 12 = 120$ N.
